# Atman

## Canonical Name

Atman

## Sanskrit

आत्मन्

## Transliteration

Ātman

## Śabda

आत्मन्

## Dhātu

अत् (At) — To move constantly; also connected to अन् (An) — to breathe, to live.

## Vyākaraṇa

Ātman is a masculine noun (though it refers to the genderless Self). Derived from the root at (to move) or an (to breathe). The word appears in all cases and is used reflexively ("oneself"). Pāṇini treats ātman as a reflexive pronoun in certain constructions.

## Nirukta

Yāska: "ātmā vyāpnoti iti" — that which pervades. Also: "ātmā aniti prāṇiti" — that which breathes. The Self is both the pervader and the life-breath.

## Bīja

अ (A) — the first letter of the Sanskrit alphabet, representing the unmanifest source. In the Gītā (10.33), Kṛṣṇa declares "akṣarāṇām akāro'smi" — among letters I am the letter A.

## Tattva

Ātma-Tattva — the principle of pure consciousness and selfhood. In Advaita: Ātman is identical with Brahman (Aham Brahmāsmi). In Sāṃkhya: Ātman (Puruṣa) is pure consciousness, eternally distinct from Prakṛti. In Viśiṣṭādvaita: Ātman is real but eternally dependent on and part of Brahman-Viṣṇu.

## Śakti

Cit-Śakti — the power of pure consciousness. Ātman is the seat of cit (consciousness), the second aspect of Sat-Cit-Ānanda (Being-Consciousness-Bliss).

## Literal Meaning

The Self; the soul; the innermost essence of a being.

## Functional Meaning

Ātman is the eternal, unchanging Self underlying individual existence. It is the witness (sākṣī) of all mental and physical activity, never itself modified. The Upaniṣads teach that Ātman is not the body, not the mind, not the intellect, not the ego — it is the pure awareness in which all these appear. The realization of Ātman as identical with Brahman (Aham Brahmāsmi) is the goal of Advaita Vedānta.

## Ontology

In Advaita Vedānta (Śaṅkara): Ātman = Brahman; the apparent difference is due to avidyā (ignorance). The mahāvākyas (great sayings) express this identity: "Aham Brahmāsmi," "Tat tvam asi," "Prajñānam Brahma," "Ayam Ātmā Brahma." In Sāṃkhya: Ātman (Puruṣa) is one of infinite individual consciousnesses, eternally distinct from Prakṛti. In Viśiṣṭādvaita: Ātman is real, individual, and eternally a part (aṃśa) of Brahman-Viṣṇu. In Dvaita (Madhva): Ātman is eternally distinct from Brahman; five eternal distinctions (pañca-bheda) are real.

## Cosmology

In Purāṇic cosmology: the individual ātman (jīvātman) is a spark of the universal Paramātman. The ātman transmigrates through the fourteen lokas according to karma. In Sāṃkhya cosmology: Puruṣa (Ātman) is the passive witness; Prakṛti (matter) evolves the universe for Puruṣa's experience and eventual liberation.

## Psychology

Ātman is the deepest layer of the self, beyond the five koshas (sheaths). In Yoga psychology: the ātman is the sākṣī (witness) that observes the modifications of the mind (citta-vṛttis) without being affected. The goal of yoga is to still the mind so the ātman shines in its own nature (svarūpa). The Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad describes four states of consciousness (waking, dreaming, deep sleep, turīya) and identifies Ātman with the fourth state (turīya) that underlies all three.

## Governance

The concept of ātman in governance: the ruler who recognizes the ātman in all beings governs with compassion and justice. The Arthaśāstra's concept of rāja-dharma is grounded in the king's recognition of his own ātman and its reflection in all subjects. Aśoka's transformation after Kalinga was described in terms of recognizing the ātman in the suffering of others.

## Medicine

In Āyurveda: the ātman is the ultimate cause of life (jīvana-hetu). Disease occurs when the ātman's connection to the body is disturbed. The concept of ātma-jñāna (self-knowledge) is considered the highest medicine. Caraka Saṃhitā states that the physician who knows the ātman can heal at the deepest level.

## Mathematics

The concept of ātman in mathematics: the Upaniṣadic teaching "ekam evādvitīyam" (one without a second) is the mathematical statement of non-duality. The concept of infinity (ananta) in Indian mathematics is connected to the infinite nature of Ātman-Brahman. Zero (śūnya) in Indian mathematics represents the void from which the ātman emerges.

## Astronomy

In Jyotiṣa: the Sun (Sūrya) is the cosmic symbol of Ātman — the self-luminous source of all light. The Sun's position in the birth chart (Sūrya-rāśi) represents the ātman's expression in this life. The concept of Sūrya as Ātman appears in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.

## Metallurgy

In alchemical traditions (Rasaśāstra): gold (suvarṇa) is the metal of the ātman — pure, unchanging, self-luminous. The alchemical goal of transmuting base metals to gold mirrors the spiritual goal of realizing the ātman beneath the base ego.

## Ritual

The Upanayana (sacred thread ceremony) initiates the student into the knowledge of Ātman. The Mahāvākya "Tat tvam asi" is transmitted from teacher to student as the core teaching. The Śrāddha ritual is based on the belief in the ātman's continuity after death. The Ahaṃgrahopāsanā (meditation on "I am Brahman") is the primary ātman-realization practice.

## Symbolism

The flame (dīpa) symbolizes Ātman — self-luminous, unaffected by wind (worldly disturbances). The sky (ākāśa) symbolizes Ātman's all-pervading, uncontained nature. The mirror symbolizes the mind reflecting the ātman's light. The lotus in the heart (hṛdaya-puṇḍarīka) is the seat of the ātman in Upaniṣadic symbolism.

## Related Deities

- Sūrya (the Sun — cosmic symbol of Ātman's self-luminosity)
- Śiva (as Paramātman — the universal Self)
- Viṣṇu (as Paramātman dwelling in all hearts)
- Brahmā (as Hiraṇyagarbha — the cosmic Self)

## Related Lokas

- Brahmaloka (Satyaloka) — the realm where Ātman-Brahman identity is fully realized
- Ātmaloka (the inner realm of self-realization)

## Related Koshas

- Ānandamaya Kosha (bliss sheath) — the innermost sheath, closest to Ātman
- Vijñānamaya Kosha (intellect sheath) — the sheath that can recognize Ātman
- All five koshas are sheaths that veil the Ātman

## Related Chakras

- Sahasrāra (crown chakra) — the seat of Paramātman realization
- Anāhata (heart chakra) — the seat of jīvātman (individual self)
- Ājñā (third eye) — the seat of ātma-vicāra (self-inquiry)

## Related Yantras

- Śrī Yantra (represents the Ātman-Brahman identity in geometric form)
- Bindu (the central point of any yantra — represents the ātman)

## Related Mantras

- "Aham Brahmāsmi" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10) — I am Brahman
- "Tat tvam asi" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7) — That thou art
- "Ayam Ātmā Brahma" (Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad 1.2) — This Self is Brahman
- "So'ham" (I am That) — the natural mantra of the breath

## Related Vidyās

- Ātmavidyā (self-knowledge — the highest vidyā)
- Brahmavidyā (knowledge of Brahman = knowledge of Ātman)
- Adhyātma Vidyā (inner science of the Self)

## Related Śāstras

- Upaniṣads (primary source — especially Bṛhadāraṇyaka, Chāndogya, Māṇḍūkya, Kaṭha, Muṇḍaka)
- Brahma Sūtras (Bādarāyaṇa)
- Bhagavad Gītā (Chapter 2 — Sāṃkhya Yoga; Chapter 13 — Kṣetra-Kṣetrajña)
- Vivekacūḍāmaṇi (Śaṅkara)

## Traditional Interpretations

- Advaita Vedānta (Śaṅkara): Ātman = Brahman; difference is illusory (vivartavāda)
- Viśiṣṭādvaita (Rāmānuja): Ātman is real, individual, and eternally part of Brahman; difference is real (pariṇāmavāda)
- Dvaita (Madhva): Ātman is eternally distinct from Brahman; five eternal differences are real
- Sāṃkhya: Ātman (Puruṣa) is pure consciousness, eternally distinct from Prakṛti
- Buddhism: Anātman (no-self) — the Buddha denied a permanent, unchanging self
- Jainism: Jīva (soul) is real, individual, and capable of liberation; similar to but distinct from Vedic Ātman

## Historical Evolution

- Ṛgvedic period: Ātman primarily means "breath" or "life-force"
- Atharvaveda: Ātman begins to acquire the meaning of "self"
- Early Upaniṣads (Bṛhadāraṇyaka, Chāndogya): Ātman = Brahman identity established
- Middle Upaniṣads (Kaṭha, Muṇḍaka): Ātman as the inner controller (antaryāmin)
- Later Upaniṣads: Ātman doctrine fully systematized
- Śaṅkara (8th century CE): Advaita interpretation — Ātman = Brahman
- Rāmānuja (11th century CE): Viśiṣṭādvaita — Ātman as part of Brahman
- Madhva (13th century CE): Dvaita — Ātman eternally distinct from Brahman

# Shakti

## Canonical Name

Shakti

## Sanskrit

शक्ति

## Transliteration

Śakti

## Śabda

शक्ति

## Dhātu

शक् (Śak) — To be able, to have power, to be capable.

## Vyākaraṇa

Śakti is a feminine noun, i-stem declension. Derived from the root śak (to be able) with the suffix -ti. The feminine gender is significant — power in the Indian tradition is inherently feminine.

## Nirukta

"Śaknoti iti śaktiḥ" — that which is capable, that which has power. Śakti is both the power itself and the Goddess who embodies that power.

## Bīja

ह्रीं (Hrīm) — the primary bīja of Śakti. Also क्रीं (Krīm) — the bīja of Kālī-Śakti; ऐं (Aim) — the bīja of Sarasvatī-Śakti; श्रीं (Śrīm) — the bīja of Lakṣmī-Śakti.

## Tattva

Śakti-Tattva — the principle of divine power and creative energy. In Śākta philosophy: Śakti is the ultimate reality — Brahman as dynamic power. In Śaiva philosophy: Śakti is Śiva's inseparable power — "Śivaḥ śaktyā yukto yadi bhavati śaktaḥ prabhavitum" (Śiva united with Śakti is capable of creating — Soundaryalaharī 1).

## Śakti

Śakti is itself the principle of śakti — it is self-referential. The three primary śaktis: Icchā-Śakti (will-power), Jñāna-Śakti (knowledge-power), Kriyā-Śakti (action-power).

## Literal Meaning

Power; energy; capability; the Goddess; the divine feminine principle.

## Functional Meaning

Śakti is the dynamic, creative, and liberating power of the universe. It is the feminine principle that activates the masculine principle (Śiva/Puruṣa). Without Śakti, Śiva is śava (a corpse) — inert. Śakti manifests as the three primary powers: Icchā (will), Jñāna (knowledge), and Kriyā (action). In the individual, Śakti manifests as kuṇḍalinī — the dormant power at the base of the spine that, when awakened, leads to liberation.

## Ontology

In Śākta philosophy: Śakti is the ultimate reality — Brahman as dynamic power. The Goddess (Devī) is not a secondary deity but the supreme reality. In Kashmir Śaivism: Śakti is Śiva's inseparable power — the universe is Śiva-Śakti's dance. In Advaita: Śakti is Brahman's māyā-śakti — the creative power of the absolute. In Sāṃkhya: Prakṛti is the equivalent of Śakti — the primal creative power.

## Cosmology

In Śākta cosmology: the universe is the Goddess's body — she is both the creator and the creation. The Devī Māhātmya describes Śakti as the power that creates, preserves, and dissolves the universe. The concept of Śakti-pīṭhas (power seats) — 51 or 108 sacred sites where the Goddess's power is concentrated.

## Psychology

Śakti as psychological principle: the three śaktis (icchā, jñāna, kriyā) correspond to will, intellect, and action in the individual. Kuṇḍalinī-śakti is the psychological-spiritual power that, when awakened through yoga, transforms consciousness. The concept of śakti-pāta (descent of grace) — the Guru's transmission of śakti to the student.

## Governance

The concept of Śakti in governance: the ruler's power (rāja-śakti) is a manifestation of divine Śakti. The Arthaśāstra describes three types of royal power: prabhāva-śakti (power of majesty), mantra-śakti (power of counsel), utsāha-śakti (power of energy). The concept of rāṣṭra-śakti (national power) in Indian political philosophy.

## Medicine

In Āyurveda: Śakti is the vital power (ojas) — the refined essence of all bodily tissues. The concept of śakti in Āyurvedic therapy: building ojas (vital power) through proper diet, lifestyle, and herbs. The concept of śakti-vardhana (power enhancement) in Āyurvedic medicine.

## Mathematics

The concept of Śakti in mathematics: the power function (śakti) in Indian mathematics — the concept of raising a number to a power. The Bījaganita (algebra) of Bhāskara uses śakti in the sense of "square" (the power of a number).

## Astronomy

In Jyotiṣa: Śakti is associated with the Moon (Candra) and Venus (Śukra) — the feminine planets. The concept of graha-śakti (planetary power) — each planet has its own śakti. The nakṣatra Śakti is associated with specific astrological powers.

## Metallurgy

In alchemical traditions: Śakti is the feminine principle in alchemy — sulfur (gandhaka) is the Śakti to mercury's (pārada) Śiva. The union of mercury and sulfur is the alchemical Śiva-Śakti union. The concept of dhātu-śakti (power of metals) — each metal has its own śakti.

## Ritual

The Śakti-pūjā (worship of the Goddess) is the primary Śākta ritual. The Navārātra (nine nights of the Goddess) is the primary Śākta festival. The concept of śakti-upāsanā (worship of power) — using the Goddess's power for liberation. The Tantric ritual of śakti-sādhana (practice with the Goddess's power).

## Symbolism

The triangle (trikona) pointing downward symbolizes Śakti — the feminine, receptive, creative power. The lotus symbolizes Śakti's creative power — blooming from the waters of consciousness. The lion (siṃha) is Śakti's vehicle — representing her power over the ego. The trident (triśūla) represents Śakti's three powers (icchā, jñāna, kriyā).

# Ahimsa

## Canonical Name

Ahimsa

## Sanskrit

अहिंसा

## Transliteration

Ahimsa

## Literal Meaning

Non-violence; non-harm; non-injury. From Sanskrit a (not) + himsa (violence, harm, injury).

## Ahimsa Paramo Dharma

The phrase **Ahimsa Paramo Dharma** (अहिंसा परमो धर्मः) means:

**"Non-violence is the highest dharma."**

- Ahimsa = non-violence
- Paramo = highest, supreme
- Dharma = duty, righteousness, cosmic order

This maxim appears in the Mahabharata (Anushasana Parva 115.1) and is one of the most cited ethical statements in Indian tradition. The full verse continues: "Ahimsa paramo dharma, tatha ahimsa paramo tapah" — Non-violence is the highest dharma; non-violence is the highest austerity.

## Functional Meaning

Ahimsa is the principle of not causing harm to any living being — in thought, word, or action. It is the foundational ethical principle shared across Hindu, Jain, and Buddhist traditions. In Jainism, ahimsa is the first and supreme vow. In Yoga, ahimsa is the first of the five Yamas (ethical restraints) in Patanjali's Ashtanga Yoga. In the Mahabharata, ahimsa is declared the highest dharma.

## Jain Teaching on Ahimsa

The Acharanga Sutra (the oldest Jain canonical text) states the core teaching of ahimsa:

"All beings desire to live. None wishes to die. Therefore, a wise person does not kill, nor causes others to kill, nor consents to killing."

The Five Great Vows (Mahavrata) for Jain monks place Ahimsa first:
1. Ahimsa — Non-violence toward all living beings
2. Satya — Absolute truthfulness
3. Asteya — Non-stealing
4. Brahmacharya — Celibacy
5. Aparigraha — Complete non-possessiveness

UniGuru Citation: Acharanga Sutra, Book 1, Lecture 7; Sacred Books of the East, Vol. 22, Jacobi translation

## Yoga Teaching on Ahimsa

In Patanjali's Yoga Sutras (2.30), Ahimsa is the first of the five Yamas:
"Ahimsa-satya-asteya-brahmacharya-aparigraha yamah" — Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness are the five restraints.

Patanjali states (Yoga Sutras 2.35): "Ahimsa-pratishthayam tat-sannidhau vaira-tyagah" — When one is established in non-violence, all enmity is abandoned in one's presence.

## Dharma Connection

The Mahabharata (Anushasana Parva) states: "Ahimsa paramo dharma" — Non-violence is the highest dharma. The Caraka Samhita (Ayurvedic text) states that the physician's svadharma includes ahimsa (non-harm) as the first ethical principle. Dharma.md cross-references Ahimsa as a related concept.

## Cosmology and Ethics

Ahimsa operates at multiple levels:
- Physical: not harming the body of any being
- Verbal: not speaking words that harm
- Mental: not harboring harmful thoughts

In Jain cosmology, every act of violence (himsa) generates karma that binds the soul. Ahimsa is therefore both an ethical principle and a metaphysical necessity for liberation (moksha).

## Related Concepts

- Dharma (Ahimsa paramo dharma — non-violence is the highest dharma)
- Karma (violence generates binding karma)

# Purusha

## Canonical Name

Purusha

## Sanskrit

पुरुष

## Transliteration

Puruṣa

## Śabda

पुरुष

## Dhātu

पुर् (Pur) — To fill, to precede; also पुरि शेते (Puri śete) — that which lies in the city (the body). Puruṣa is "that which fills" or "that which dwells in the city (body)."

## Vyākaraṇa

Puruṣa is a masculine noun. It has multiple meanings: (1) the cosmic person (Ṛgveda 10.90), (2) the individual soul (Sāṃkhya), (3) the supreme being (Viṣṇu/Brahman), (4) a human being (man).

## Nirukta

Yāska: "puri śayānāt puruṣaḥ" — that which lies in the city (body). The soul dwells in the body as a person dwells in a city.

## Bīja

ॐ (Om) — the primordial sound of Puruṣa. Also सोऽहम् (So'ham) — the natural mantra of Puruṣa (I am That).

## Tattva

Puruṣa-Tattva — the principle of pure consciousness and cosmic personhood. In Sāṃkhya: Puruṣa is one of the two ultimate realities (along with Prakṛti). It is pure consciousness (cit), eternally free, and the witness of Prakṛti's evolution.

## Śakti

Puruṣa is the śaktimān (the possessor of śakti) — Prakṛti is his śakti. Puruṣa himself is pure consciousness without activity — his presence activates Prakṛti.

## Literal Meaning

The cosmic person; the individual soul; the supreme being; a human being.

## Functional Meaning

Puruṣa is the principle of pure consciousness that witnesses Prakṛti's evolution without being affected by it. In Sāṃkhya: Puruṣa is the eternal, unchanging witness — it does not act, does not create, does not suffer. It is the pure light of consciousness in which Prakṛti's evolution appears. Liberation (kaivalya) is Puruṣa's recognition of its eternal distinction from Prakṛti. In the Ṛgveda (10.90), the cosmic Puruṣa is the primordial being from whose sacrifice the universe was created.

## Ontology

In Sāṃkhya: Puruṣa is one of the two ultimate realities — pure consciousness, eternally distinct from Prakṛti. There are infinite individual Puruṣas (unlike Advaita's one Ātman). In Advaita: Puruṣa = Ātman = Brahman — the one universal consciousness. In Viśiṣṭādvaita: Puruṣa is the individual soul (jīva) — real, individual, and eternally part of Brahman-Viṣṇu. In Yoga: Puruṣa is the witness-consciousness (sākṣī) that observes the mind's modifications.

## Cosmology

In Vedic cosmology: the Puruṣa Sūkta (Ṛgveda 10.90) describes the cosmic Puruṣa as the primordial being with a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, a thousand feet — encompassing the entire universe. From the sacrifice of the cosmic Puruṣa, the universe was created: the moon from his mind, the sun from his eye, Indra and Agni from his mouth, Vāyu from his breath, the sky from his navel, the earth from his feet.

## Psychology

Puruṣa as psychological principle: the witness-consciousness (sākṣī) that observes all mental activity without being affected. The goal of yoga is to identify with Puruṣa (the witness) rather than with Prakṛti (the mind and body). The concept of puruṣa-viveka (discrimination of Puruṣa from Prakṛti) is the central practice of Sāṃkhya-Yoga.

## Governance

The concept of Puruṣa in governance: the ideal ruler is one who governs from the standpoint of Puruṣa — as a witness, without personal attachment. The concept of rāja-puruṣa (the royal person) — the king as the embodiment of the cosmic Puruṣa in the kingdom.

## Medicine

In Āyurveda: Puruṣa is the conscious principle that animates the body. The concept of puruṣa-prakṛti (the individual's consciousness-nature combination) determines health and disease tendencies. The Caraka Saṃhitā describes the physician's task as restoring the harmony between Puruṣa and Prakṛti in the patient.

## Mathematics

The concept of Puruṣa in mathematics: the concept of the observer in quantum mechanics has been compared to the Sāṃkhya Puruṣa — the observer who does not interfere but whose presence affects the observed. This remains a philosophical analogy.

## Astronomy

In Jyotiṣa: Puruṣa is associated with the Sun (Sūrya) — the cosmic witness, the source of light. The concept of Kālapuruṣa (the person of time) — the zodiac is mapped onto the body of the cosmic Puruṣa.

## Metallurgy

In alchemical traditions: Puruṣa is the gold (suvarṇa) — the pure, unchanging metal that represents pure consciousness. The alchemical goal of transmuting base metals to gold mirrors the spiritual goal of recognizing Puruṣa beneath Prakṛti.

## Ritual

The Puruṣa Sūkta (Ṛgveda 10.90) is recited in all major Vedic rituals. The concept of puruṣa-medha (human sacrifice) — a symbolic ritual in which the cosmic Puruṣa's sacrifice is re-enacted. The concept of puruṣa-sūkta-pāṭha (recitation of the Puruṣa Sūkta) as a daily ritual.

## Symbolism

The cosmic person (viśvarūpa) symbolizes Puruṣa — the universe as the body of the cosmic being. The sun symbolizes Puruṣa — the self-luminous witness. The mirror symbolizes Puruṣa — it reflects all without being affected.

# Brahman

## Canonical Name

Brahman

## Sanskrit

ब्रह्मन्

## Transliteration

Brahman

## Śabda

ब्रह्मन्

## Dhātu

बृह् (Bṛh) — To expand, to grow, to be great.

## Vyākaraṇa

Brahman is a neuter noun (not to be confused with Brahmā, the masculine creator deity, or Brāhmaṇa, the priestly class). Derived from the root bṛh with the suffix -man. The neuter gender indicates that Brahman transcends all categories including gender.

## Nirukta

Yāska: "bṛhati iti brahma" — that which is great, that which expands. Brahman is the infinitely expanding reality that underlies all existence.

## Bīja

ॐ (Om/Auṃ) — the primordial sound that is the sonic form of Brahman. The Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad opens: "Auṃ ity etad akṣaram idaṃ sarvam" — Om, this syllable is all this.

## Tattva

Brahma-Tattva — the principle of absolute, infinite, self-luminous reality. Brahman is described as Sat-Cit-Ānanda (Being-Consciousness-Bliss) — not three qualities but three aspects of one indivisible reality.

## Śakti

Brahman's śakti is Māyā — the creative power that projects the apparent multiplicity of the universe. In Śākta traditions, Brahman without Śakti is inert (śava); Brahman with Śakti is Śiva (the living absolute).

## Literal Meaning

The Absolute; the Infinite; the Ultimate Reality; the Ground of Being.

## Functional Meaning

Brahman is the infinite, eternal, unchanging absolute reality that is the ground of all existence. It is both the material cause (upādāna-kāraṇa) and the efficient cause (nimitta-kāraṇa) of the universe. Brahman is described via two approaches: Nirguṇa Brahman (without attributes — the absolute beyond all description) and Saguṇa Brahman (with attributes — the personal God, Īśvara). The Upaniṣads teach that Brahman is identical with Ātman (the individual Self).

## Ontology

In Advaita Vedānta (Śaṅkara): Brahman alone is real (Brahma satyam); the world is appearance (jagat mithyā); the individual self is Brahman (jīvo brahmaiva nāparaḥ). In Viśiṣṭādvaita (Rāmānuja): Brahman is real, personal (Viṣṇu), and the universe and souls are Brahman's body. In Dvaita (Madhva): Brahman (Viṣṇu) is real and eternally distinct from souls and world. In Śaiva Siddhānta: Brahman is Śiva, the supreme reality with infinite śaktis.

## Cosmology

Brahman is the source, sustainer, and dissolution point of all universes. The Taittirīya Upaniṣad: "yato vā imāni bhūtāni jāyante" — from which all beings are born, by which they live, into which they return — that is Brahman. The Purāṇas describe Brahman as the ocean from which the universe arises like waves. The concept of Brahmaṇḍa (Brahman's egg) is the cosmic egg from which the universe hatches.

## Psychology

Brahman as psychological reality: the deepest layer of consciousness is Brahman. In Yoga psychology, the state of samādhi (absorption) is the direct experience of Brahman. The Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad identifies Brahman with the fourth state of consciousness (turīya) that underlies waking, dreaming, and deep sleep. The experience of Brahman is described as "neti neti" (not this, not this) — Brahman cannot be grasped by the mind but is the ground of the mind.

## Governance

The concept of Brahman in governance: the ideal ruler is one who has realized Brahman and governs from that realization. The Arthaśāstra's concept of the philosopher-king parallels the Upaniṣadic ideal of the Brahman-realized ruler. The concept of Brahma-rāṣṭra (the kingdom of Brahman) appears in Vedic literature as the ideal polity.

## Medicine

In Āyurveda: Brahman is the ultimate source of health (ārogya). The concept of Brahma-cakra (the cycle of Brahman) underlies the Āyurvedic understanding of the body as a microcosm of the universe. The highest healing is Brahma-jñāna (knowledge of Brahman) which removes the root cause of all disease — avidyā (ignorance).

## Mathematics

The concept of Brahman in mathematics: Brahman as the infinite (ananta) is the philosophical basis for the Indian mathematical concept of infinity. The concept of śūnya (zero) as the void from which all numbers emerge mirrors the Brahman-as-source concept. The Upaniṣadic statement "pūrṇam adaḥ pūrṇam idam" (that is full, this is full) is a mathematical statement about the nature of infinity.

## Astronomy

In Jyotiṣa: Brahman is identified with the cosmic space (ākāśa) in which all celestial bodies move. The concept of Brahma-muhūrta (the hour of Brahman — 1.5 hours before sunrise) is the most auspicious time for spiritual practice. The Milky Way (Ākāśagaṅgā) is considered the visible form of Brahman's cosmic body.

## Metallurgy

In alchemical traditions: Brahman is the philosophical gold (parama-suvarṇa) — the ultimate substance that all metals aspire to become. The alchemical process of transmutation mirrors the spiritual process of realizing Brahman beneath the apparent multiplicity of substances.

## Ritual

The Brahma-yajña (sacrifice to Brahman) is the daily recitation of the Vedas — the highest ritual act. The Upanayana ceremony initiates the student into the study of Brahman. The Mahāvākyas are transmitted in ritual contexts as the direct teaching of Brahman. The concept of Brahma-vidyā (knowledge of Brahman) is the ultimate goal of all Vedic ritual.

## Symbolism

Om (ॐ) is the primary symbol of Brahman — the sound of the universe. The infinite space (ākāśa) symbolizes Brahman's all-pervading nature. The ocean symbolizes Brahman — waves (individual beings) arise from and return to the ocean. The sun symbolizes Nirguṇa Brahman — self-luminous, the source of all light. The bindu (point) in the center of a yantra represents Brahman as the source of all manifestation.

# Maya

## Canonical Name

Maya

## Sanskrit

माया

## Transliteration

Māyā

## Śabda

माया

## Dhātu

मा (Mā) — To measure, to create, to construct. Māyā is "that which measures out" or "that which creates the appearance of measure and form."

## Vyākaraṇa

Māyā is a feminine noun. Derived from the root mā (to measure/create) with the suffix -yā. In Vedic usage, māyā means "supernatural power" or "creative magic." In Advaita Vedānta, it acquires the technical meaning of "cosmic illusion."

## Nirukta

"Māyate iti māyā" — that which measures/creates. Also: "mā — not, yā — that which is" — that which is not (the appearance of what is not real). The second etymology is a later philosophical interpretation.

## Bīja

ह्रीं (Hrīm) — the bīja of Māyā-Śakti in Tantric traditions. Hrīm is the bīja of the Goddess as the creative power of illusion and liberation.

## Tattva

Māyā-Tattva — the principle of creative illusion and cosmic appearance. In Advaita: Māyā is the power of Brahman that projects the apparent multiplicity of the universe. In Kashmir Śaivism: Māyā is one of the five kañcukas (coverings) that limit the universal consciousness.

## Śakti

Māyā-Śakti — the creative and concealing power. Māyā has two functions: āvaraṇa-śakti (concealing power — it conceals Brahman) and vikṣepa-śakti (projecting power — it projects the apparent world).

## Literal Meaning

Illusion; creative power; supernatural power; the cosmic appearance.

## Functional Meaning

Māyā is the cosmic power that creates the appearance of multiplicity in the non-dual Brahman. It is neither real (sat) nor unreal (asat) — it is anirvachanīya (indescribable). Māyā operates through avidyā (ignorance) at the individual level and through the cosmic creative power at the universal level. Liberation (mokṣa) is the transcendence of māyā through jñāna (knowledge).

## Ontology

In Advaita Vedānta (Śaṅkara): Māyā is the power of Brahman that creates the appearance of the world. It is neither real nor unreal — it is mithyā (apparent). The world is not non-existent (it appears) but not ultimately real (it is not Brahman). In Viśiṣṭādvaita (Rāmānuja): Māyā is Viṣṇu's creative power — real, not illusory. In Dvaita (Madhva): Māyā is Viṣṇu's power — the world created by māyā is real. In Kashmir Śaivism: Māyā is one of the thirty-six tattvas — a real power of Śiva that limits universal consciousness.

## Cosmology

In Purāṇic cosmology: Māyā is Viṣṇu's creative power (Yoga-Māyā) that maintains the cosmic illusion. The Devī Māhātmya describes Māyā as the Goddess herself — the cosmic creative power. In Sāṃkhya: Prakṛti (primal matter) is the equivalent of Māyā — the creative power that produces the universe for Puruṣa's experience.

## Psychology

Māyā as psychological principle: avidyā (individual ignorance) is the psychological form of cosmic māyā. The three psychological functions of māyā: āvaraṇa (concealment of the true Self), vikṣepa (projection of the false self), and mala (impurity). Liberation requires the removal of māyā through viveka (discrimination) and vairāgya (dispassion).

## Governance

The concept of māyā in governance: the ruler who is deluded by māyā governs for personal gain rather than dharma. The Arthaśāstra warns against the māyā of power — the illusion that the king is the ultimate authority. The concept of rāja-māyā (royal illusion) — the danger of rulers believing their own propaganda.

## Medicine

In Āyurveda: māyā (illusion/delusion) is a cause of mental disease (mānasa-roga). The concept of prajñāparādha (crime against wisdom) — acting against one's better knowledge — is the Āyurvedic equivalent of māyā's concealing function.

## Mathematics

The concept of māyā in mathematics: the appearance of multiplicity from unity mirrors the mathematical concept of differentiation. The concept of māyā as "measurement" (from the root mā) connects to the mathematical act of measuring — imposing finite measure on the infinite.

## Astronomy

In Jyotiṣa: Māyā is associated with the Moon (Candra) — the planet of illusion, reflection, and the mind. The Moon's phases represent māyā's changing appearances. The concept of graha-māyā (planetary illusion) — the apparent retrograde motion of planets is a form of māyā.

## Metallurgy

In alchemical traditions: māyā is the appearance of base metals as gold — the alchemist's task is to see through māyā to the true nature of substances. The concept of māyā in metallurgy: the surface appearance of a metal (its color, luster) may conceal its true nature.

## Ritual

The concept of māyā in ritual: ritual itself operates within māyā — it uses the apparent world to point beyond it. The concept of māyā-pūjā (worship through the apparent) — using forms, images, and rituals to transcend form. The Tantric tradition explicitly works with māyā — using the apparent world as the path to liberation.

## Symbolism

The veil symbolizes māyā — it conceals what is behind it. The mirror symbolizes māyā — it creates an apparent reflection that is not the original. The dream symbolizes māyā — vivid and real while experienced, but recognized as unreal upon waking. The magician (māyāvī) symbolizes māyā's creative power.

## Related Deities

- Devī/Mahāmāyā (the Goddess as the cosmic māyā-power)
- Viṣṇu (Yoga-Māyā — his creative power)
- Śiva (Māyā as his śakti)
- Durgā (the Goddess who wields māyā to protect dharma)

## Related Lokas

- All lokas are within māyā — they are māyā's projections
- Brahmaloka is beyond māyā

## Related Koshas

- All five koshas are māyā's projections
- Ānandamaya Kosha is the subtlest form of māyā

## Related Chakras

- Ājñā (third eye) — the chakra of discrimination that sees through māyā
- Sahasrāra (crown) — beyond māyā

## Related Yantras

- Śrī Yantra (the geometric form of Māyā-Śakti's creative power)
- Hrīm Yantra (the yantra of Māyā-bīja)

## Related Mantras

- "Hrīm" (the bīja of Māyā-Śakti)
- "Om aim hrīm klīm cāmuṇḍāyai vicce" (Navārṇa Mantra — invoking the Goddess beyond māyā)

- Śakti Vidyā (the science of the Goddess as māyā-power)

- Viśiṣṭādvaita: Māyā is Viṣṇu's real creative power — the world is real
- Dvaita: Māyā is Viṣṇu's power — the world created by māyā is real
- Śākta: Māyā is the Goddess herself — the creative power of the universe

## Historical Evolution

- Upaniṣadic period: Māyā as the creative power of Brahman
- Gauḍapāda (7th century CE): Māyā as the basis of the apparent world
- Śaṅkara (8th century CE): Māyā as cosmic illusion — the central concept of Advaita

[EXPERIMENTAL — NOT CANONICAL] Some philosophers of mind propose that the Advaita concept of māyā anticipates the modern philosophical problem of the "veil of perception" — the question of whether we perceive reality directly or only its appearances. This remains a philosophical analogy.

# Om

## Canonical Name

Om

## Sanskrit

ॐ

## Transliteration

Om (also Auṃ)

## Śabda

ॐ

## Dhātu

अव् (Av) — To protect, to pervade. Some traditions derive Om from the root av (to protect) or from the three letters A-U-M representing creation, preservation, dissolution.

## Vyākaraṇa

Om is classified as a praṇava (primordial sound) and an avyaya (indeclinable). It is not declined like ordinary nouns. Pāṇini treats it as a sacred syllable (maṅgala-vācaka). The written form ॐ is a ligature of the three letters A, U, M with the anusvāra (nasal resonance) and the bindu (point of silence above).

## Nirukta

Yāska: Om is the name of Brahman. The Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad: "Auṃ ity etad akṣaram idaṃ sarvam" — Om, this syllable is all this. The three letters represent the three states of consciousness (waking, dreaming, deep sleep) and the three worlds.

## Bīja

ॐ itself is the mahā-bīja (great seed syllable) — the source of all other bīja mantras.

## Tattva

Praṇava-Tattva — the principle of the primordial sound. Om is the sonic form of Brahman — the vibration from which the universe emerges and into which it dissolves.

## Śakti

Nāda-Śakti — the power of primordial sound. Om is the first vibration of Śakti — the creative power of the universe expressed as sound.

## Literal Meaning

The primordial sound; the syllable of Brahman; yes; so be it; the affirmation of existence.

## Functional Meaning

Om is the sonic representation of Brahman — the absolute reality expressed as vibration. It is used as a prefix to all mantras, prayers, and sacred texts. The Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad teaches that Om encompasses all of time (past, present, future) and all states of consciousness. Meditation on Om leads to the direct experience of Brahman.

## Ontology

In Advaita Vedānta: Om = Brahman; meditating on Om is meditating on Brahman. In Mīmāṃsā: Om is the eternal, self-existent sound (śabda-brahman) — the Vedas are the eternal sound of Brahman. In Tantra: Om is the mahā-bīja from which all other bīja mantras emerge. In Yoga: Om is the name of Īśvara (God) — "tasya vācakaḥ praṇavaḥ" (Yoga Sūtras 1.27).

## Cosmology

In Vedic cosmology: Om is the sound of the universe — the cosmic vibration (nāda-brahman) from which all creation emerges. The Purāṇas describe Brahmā creating the universe by uttering Om. The concept of nāda (sound) as the first manifestation of Brahman underlies the cosmological significance of Om.

## Psychology

Meditation on Om (Om-japa, Om-dhyāna) is the primary practice for stilling the mind. The Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad maps the four parts of Om (A, U, M, silence) onto the four states of consciousness (waking, dreaming, deep sleep, turīya). The practice of Om-kāra-dhyāna (meditation on Om) leads through all four states to the recognition of Ātman = Brahman.

## Governance

Om as the foundation of governance: all royal proclamations and sacred oaths begin with Om. The concept of Om as the affirmation of cosmic order (ṛta) underlies its use in governance contexts.

## Medicine

In Āyurveda: Om is the primordial sound therapy. The vibration of Om is used in mantra-cikitsā (mantra therapy). Research suggests that chanting Om produces specific neurological effects — calming the nervous system and reducing stress.

## Mathematics

The concept of Om in mathematics: Om as the symbol of infinity (ananta) — the sound that contains all sounds. The bindu (point) above the Om symbol represents the mathematical point — dimensionless, yet the source of all dimensions.

## Astronomy

In Jyotiṣa: Om is associated with the Sun (Sūrya) — the cosmic source of light and life. The Gāyatrī Mantra begins with Om and is addressed to the Sun. The concept of Om as the sound of the cosmic cycles (yugas, kalpas).

## Metallurgy

In ritual metallurgy: Om is inscribed on sacred objects to infuse them with divine power. The concept of Om as the mantra of consecration — all sacred metal objects are consecrated with Om.

## Ritual

Om begins and ends all Vedic rituals, mantras, and prayers. The Vedic tradition: "Om iti brahma" — Om is Brahman. The daily practice of Om-kāra-japa (repetition of Om) is the foundational spiritual practice. The concept of praṇava-upāsanā (worship through Om) is described in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.

## Symbolism

The written symbol ॐ represents: A (waking state/creation), U (dreaming state/preservation), M (deep sleep/dissolution), the curve above (māyā/illusion), the dot (turīya/liberation), the silence after (Brahman). The three curves represent the three states of consciousness. The dot represents the fourth state (turīya) — pure awareness.

- Śiva (Om Namaḥ Śivāya begins with Om)

# Rta

## Canonical Name

Rta

## Sanskrit

ऋत

## Transliteration

Ṛta

## Śabda

ऋत

## Dhātu

ऋ (Ṛ) — To go, to move, to flow. Ṛta is "that which has moved/flowed in the right way" — the right order of things.

## Vyākaraṇa

Ṛta is a neuter noun derived from the past passive participle of the root ṛ (to go/flow). It means "that which has gone rightly" — the right order, the truth, the cosmic law.

## Nirukta

Yāska: "ṛtam — satyam" — Ṛta is truth. The cosmic truth that underlies all existence. Ṛta is both the cosmic order and the truth that expresses it.

## Bīja

ऋ (Ṛ) — the vowel ṛ itself is the bīja of cosmic order and right movement.

## Tattva

Ṛta-Tattva — the principle of cosmic truth and right order. Ṛta is the Vedic precursor to Dharma — the cosmic law that governs all existence before it was articulated as ethical principle.

## Śakti

Ṛta-Śakti — the power of cosmic truth. The śakti that maintains the right order of the universe — the movements of the sun, the seasons, the moral order of human society.

## Literal Meaning

Cosmic order; truth; right; the law of the universe.

## Functional Meaning

Ṛta is the Vedic concept of cosmic truth and right order. It governs the movements of the celestial bodies, the cycle of seasons, the moral order of human society, and the efficacy of ritual. Varuṇa is the primary guardian of Ṛta — he punishes those who violate it. Ṛta is the foundation from which Dharma (ethical order) later developed. The concept of Ṛta underlies the Vedic understanding of truth (satya) — to speak truth is to align with Ṛta.

## Ontology

In Vedic ontology: Ṛta is the cosmic law that precedes and underlies all existence. It is not created by the gods but is the principle by which the gods themselves operate. In later philosophy: Ṛta becomes Dharma (ethical order) and Satya (truth) — the two primary expressions of cosmic law.

## Cosmology

In Vedic cosmology: Ṛta governs the movements of the sun (Sūrya follows Ṛta), the cycle of seasons (ṛtu — season — derives from Ṛta), the flow of rivers, and the moral order of the universe. The concept of Ṛta-dhāman (the abode of Ṛta) — the cosmic realm where Ṛta is perfectly expressed.

## Psychology

Ṛta as psychological principle: the person who lives in alignment with Ṛta experiences inner harmony. The violation of Ṛta (anṛta — untruth, adharma) creates psychological disturbance. The concept of ṛta-cit (Ṛta-consciousness) — the mind that perceives and aligns with cosmic truth.

## Governance

Ṛta as the foundation of governance: the king who governs according to Ṛta maintains cosmic order. The concept of rāja-dharma (royal duty) is the application of Ṛta to governance. Varuṇa's role as the guardian of Ṛta is the model for the king's role as the guardian of dharma.

## Medicine

In Āyurveda: Ṛta as the right order of the body — health is the body's alignment with Ṛta. The concept of ṛtu-caryā (seasonal regimen) — living according to the seasonal Ṛta for optimal health.

## Mathematics

The concept of Ṛta in mathematics: mathematical truth (satya) is a form of Ṛta — the right order of numbers and relationships. The Vedic concept of mathematical precision in ritual (Śulbasūtras) is an expression of Ṛta.

## Astronomy

Ṛta is most directly expressed in astronomy — the right movements of celestial bodies. The concept of ṛtu (season) derives from Ṛta — the seasons are the cosmic Ṛta expressed in time. Vedic astronomy (Jyotiṣa) is the science of tracking Ṛta in the sky.

## Metallurgy

The concept of Ṛta in metallurgy: the right order of metallurgical processes — following the dharma of each metal is following its Ṛta.

## Ritual

Yajña (sacrifice) is the primary ritual expression of Ṛta — it maintains and reinforces cosmic order. ## Purpose of the Puranas

# Karma

## Canonical Name

Karma

## Sanskrit

कर्म

## Transliteration

Karma

## Śabda

कर्म

## Dhātu

कृ (Kṛ) — To do, perform, act, make.

## Vyākaraṇa

Derived from the verbal root कृ (kṛ) with the suffix -man (neuter noun). Pāṇini Ashtadhyayi 3.3.18. Karma is a neuter noun meaning "action" or "deed." In grammar, karma also denotes the object of a verb (karman = object/patient).

## Nirukta

Yāska: "kriyate anena iti karma" — that by which action is performed. The root kṛ encompasses all forms of doing, making, and performing.

## Bīja

क (Ka) — the seed syllable of action and creation in Tantric traditions. Associated with Brahmā (the creator) whose bīja is also Ka.

## Tattva

Karma-Tattva — the principle of causation through action. In Sāṃkhya: karma is the activity of the three guṇas (sattva, rajas, tamas). In Vaiśeṣika: karma is one of the seven padārthas (categories), defined as motion. In Vedānta: karma is the mechanism of saṃsāra (cycle of rebirth).

## Śakti

Kriyā-Śakti — the power of action. One of the three fundamental śaktis (icchā-jñāna-kriyā). Karma operates through kriyā-śakti as the dynamic force of manifestation.

## Literal Meaning

Action; deed; work; ritual act.

## Functional Meaning

Karma is the universal principle that every action generates corresponding consequences. It operates across three dimensions: Sañcita karma (accumulated past actions), Prārabdha karma (karma currently bearing fruit), and Āgāmi/Kriyamāṇa karma (karma being created now). The law of karma is not punishment but the natural law of cause and effect operating through consciousness.

## Ontology

In Mīmāṃsā: karma (ritual action) is the primary means of achieving dharmic results; the apūrva (unseen potency) of ritual karma persists until it bears fruit. In Advaita Vedānta: karma operates only at the vyāvahārika level; from the absolute standpoint, there is no doer, hence no karma. In Viśiṣṭādvaita: karma is real and must be exhausted through bhakti and surrender to Viṣṇu. In Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika: karma is one of seven categories of reality, defined as motion (pariṇāma).

## Cosmology

Karma drives the cycle of saṃsāra across all fourteen lokas. The Purāṇas describe karma as the mechanism by which souls transmigrate through different realms. In Jain cosmology, karma is a subtle material substance (karma-pudgala) that adheres to the soul (jīva) and determines its condition. The Bhāgavata Purāṇa describes karma as the force that maintains the cosmic order of creation, preservation, and dissolution.

## Psychology

In Yoga psychology: karma creates saṃskāras (mental impressions) and vāsanās (latent tendencies) that condition future experience. Patañjali's Yoga Sūtras 2.12-14 describe the karma-āśaya (karma-store) as the root of birth, lifespan, and experience. Karma operates through the kāraṇa-śarīra (causal body). Karma yoga (the yoga of action) transforms karma from bondage to liberation by eliminating the sense of doership (ahaṃkāra).

## Governance

Karma as social principle: the concept of karma-phala (fruit of action) underlies Indian jurisprudence. Kauṭilya's Arthaśāstra recognizes that rulers accumulate karma through their governance. The concept of rāja-dharma (royal duty) is the karmic responsibility of the king. Historical Indian governance was explicitly framed in karmic terms — Aśoka's dhamma edicts reflect karmic accountability.

## Medicine

In Āyurveda: karma is one of the causes of disease (prājñāparādha — crime against wisdom is a karmic cause). Caraka Saṃhitā identifies karma as a factor in the etiology of disease. Karmic diseases (ādhidaivika) require spiritual remedies alongside physical treatment. The concept of karma-ja-vyādhi (karma-born disease) is a distinct category in Āyurvedic pathology.

## Mathematics

The mathematical principle of karma is the law of conservation: every action has an equal and opposite reaction. Vedic mathematics (Gaṇita) treats karma as the principle of balance — equations must balance, debts must be settled. The concept of ṛṇa (debt) in Vedic mathematics mirrors the karmic debt concept.

## Astronomy

Karma in Jyotiṣa (Vedic astrology): the birth chart (janma-kuṇḍali) is considered a map of prārabdha karma. Planetary positions at birth reflect accumulated karma. The concept of daśā (planetary period) describes the timing of karmic fruition. Graha (planets) are considered agents of karma delivery.

## Metallurgy

In Viśvakarmā tradition: the karma of the craftsman (śilpin) determines the quality of the work. The concept of karma-yoga in craft: the craftsman who works without attachment to results produces the finest work. The dharma of metals (their inherent properties) must be respected — working against a metal's karma produces inferior results.

## Ritual

Karma-kāṇḍa (ritual section of the Vedas) is the primary domain of Mīmāṃsā. The sixteen saṃskāras are karmic rituals that shape the individual's karmic trajectory. Yajña (sacrifice) is the highest karmic act — it purifies accumulated karma and generates positive karma. Prāyaścitta (expiation) rituals neutralize specific karmic debts.

## Symbolism

The wheel (cakra) symbolizes karma's cyclical nature. The scales represent karmic balance. The seed (bīja) represents karma's potential — every action is a seed that will bear fruit. The mirror represents karma's reflective nature — what you do returns to you. The knot (granthi) represents karmic bondage.

## Related Deities

- Yama (Dharmarāja — lord of karmic accounting and death)
- Citragupta (Yama's scribe who records all karma)
- Śani (Saturn — the planet of karmic lessons and consequences)
- Brahmā (the creator who sets karma in motion)
- Viṣṇu (the preserver who maintains karmic order)

## Related Lokas

- Naraka (hell realms — destination of negative karma)
- Svarga (heaven realms — destination of positive karma)
- Pitṛloka (realm of ancestors — intermediate karmic state)
- Bhūloka (earth — the primary field of karmic action)

## Related Koshas

- Kāraṇa Śarīra (causal body) — the storehouse of accumulated karma (sañcita karma)
- Sūkṣma Śarīra (subtle body) — the vehicle through which karma is experienced
- Manomaya Kosha (mind sheath) — where karmic intentions originate

## Related Chakras

- Maṇipūra (solar plexus chakra) — seat of will, action, and karmic agency
- Mūlādhāra (root chakra) — seat of prārabdha karma and survival instincts
- Svādhiṣṭhāna (sacral chakra) — seat of karmic desires and creative action

## Related Yantras

- Karma Yantra (used in rituals for karmic purification)
- Śani Yantra (for mitigating difficult karmic periods)

## Related Mantras

- "Karmaṇy evādhikāras te mā phaleṣu kadācana" (Bhagavad Gītā 2.47) — You have the right to action alone, never to its fruits
- Mahāmṛtyuñjaya Mantra (for liberation from karmic death-cycle)
- Śani Mantra: "Om śam śanaiścarāya namaḥ" (for karmic lessons)

## Related Vidyās

- Karma-Yoga Vidyā (science of action without attachment)
- Jyotiṣa Vidyā (science of karmic timing)
- Prāyaścitta Vidyā (science of karmic expiation)

## Related Śāstras

- Bhagavad Gītā (Chapters 3, 4, 5 — Karma Yoga)
- Mīmāṃsā Sūtras (Jaimini) — ritual karma
- Yoga Sūtras (Patañjali) 2.12-14 — karma-āśaya
- Tattvartha Sūtra (Umāsvāti) — Jain karma doctrine
- Caraka Saṃhitā — karmic disease

## Traditional Interpretations

- Advaita Vedānta (Śaṅkara): Karma is ultimately unreal from the absolute standpoint; jñāna (knowledge) alone destroys karma
- Viśiṣṭādvaita (Rāmānuja): Karma is real and must be surrendered to Viṣṇu through prapatti (surrender)
- Dvaita (Madhva): Karma is eternally real; liberation requires Viṣṇu's grace to transcend karma
- Mīmāṃsā: Karma (ritual action) is the primary means of achieving all human goals
- Buddhism: Karma is intentional action (cetanā); it is the intention, not the act, that creates karma
- Jainism: Karma is a subtle material substance that binds the soul; liberation requires exhausting all karma through tapas (austerity)

## Historical Evolution

- Ṛgvedic period: Karma primarily means ritual action; cosmic karma (ṛta) governs the universe
- Brāhmaṇa period: Karma as ritual action is elaborated extensively; karma-kāṇḍa develops
- Upaniṣadic period: Karma as ethical-spiritual principle emerges; karma-saṃsāra connection established
- Buddhist period (500 BCE): Karma redefined as intentional action; karma-rebirth doctrine systematized
- Jain period: Karma as material substance — unique and influential formulation
- Epic-Purāṇic period: Karma as cosmic justice mechanism; karma-yoga as path to liberation
- Medieval: Karma integrated into bhakti traditions — karma surrendered to God

## Cross References

- Dharma
- Moksha
- Yoga
- Saṃskāra
- Punarjanma (rebirth)
- Ahaṃkāra (ego — the false doer)
- Vāsanā (latent tendencies)

## Open Research Questions

- Is karma a deterministic or probabilistic system? Can free will operate within karma?
- What is the relationship between Vedic karma (ritual action) and Buddhist karma (intentional action)?
- How does the Jain material karma theory relate to the Vedic subtle-body karma theory?

## Experimental Hypotheses

[EXPERIMENTAL — NOT CANONICAL] Some researchers propose that karma theory anticipates modern concepts of information conservation in physics — that the "information" of every action is preserved in the universe. This remains speculative and is not established in any canonical tradition.

## Canonical Sources

- Bhagavad Gītā 2.47, 3.5, 4.17
- Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.2.13 (karma-rebirth connection)
- Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10 (karma and rebirth)
- Yoga Sūtras 2.12-14
- Tattvartha Sūtra (Umāsvāti) — Jain karma
- Mīmāṃsā Sūtras (Jaimini)

# Prakrti

## Canonical Name

Prakrti

## Sanskrit

प्रकृति

## Transliteration

Prakṛti

## Śabda

प्रकृति

## Dhātu

प्र + कृ (Pra + Kṛ) — Pra (before, primary, forth) + Kṛ (to do, to make). The primary maker; the original nature; that which was made first.

## Vyākaraṇa

Prakṛti is a feminine noun derived from the prefix pra- and the root kṛ (to make) with the suffix -ti. The feminine gender is significant — Prakṛti is the feminine creative principle, complementary to the masculine Puruṣa.

## Nirukta

"Prakṛṣṭā kṛtiḥ prakṛtiḥ" — the primary creation. Prakṛti is the original nature from which all manifest existence emerges.

## Bīja

ह्रीं (Hrīm) — the bīja of Prakṛti as the creative power. Also क्लीं (Klīm) — the bīja of attraction and manifestation.

## Tattva

Prakṛti-Tattva — the principle of primal matter and creative nature. In Sāṃkhya: Prakṛti is one of the two ultimate realities (along with Puruṣa). It is the material cause of the universe — the primal matter from which all manifest existence evolves.

## Śakti

Prakṛti is itself the śakti — the creative power. In Śākta traditions, Prakṛti = Śakti = the Goddess. The three guṇas (sattva, rajas, tamas) are the three śaktis of Prakṛti.

## Literal Meaning

Nature; primal matter; the original creative principle; the feminine creative power.

## Functional Meaning

Prakṛti is the primal, undifferentiated matter from which the entire manifest universe evolves. In Sāṃkhya philosophy, Prakṛti consists of three guṇas (qualities): Sattva (clarity, luminosity), Rajas (activity, passion), Tamas (inertia, darkness). When the three guṇas are in perfect equilibrium, Prakṛti is unmanifest (avyakta). When the equilibrium is disturbed (by Puruṣa's proximity), Prakṛti begins to evolve the universe through twenty-three tattvas (principles).

## Ontology

In Sāṃkhya: Prakṛti is one of the two ultimate realities — it is the material cause of the universe. It is unconscious (acetana) but active. Puruṣa is conscious but inactive. The universe is the product of their interaction. In Advaita: Prakṛti = Māyā — the creative power of Brahman. In Viśiṣṭādvaita: Prakṛti is the body of Brahman-Viṣṇu — real and dependent on Brahman. In Śākta: Prakṛti = the Goddess — the supreme creative reality.

## Cosmology

In Sāṃkhya cosmology: from Prakṛti evolves Mahat (cosmic intellect), then Ahaṃkāra (ego-principle), then the five tanmātras (subtle elements), then the five mahābhūtas (gross elements), then the ten indriyas (sense and action organs), then manas (mind) — twenty-three tattvas in total. The universe is Prakṛti's evolution for Puruṣa's experience and eventual liberation.

## Psychology

Prakṛti as psychological principle: the three guṇas govern all psychological states. Sattva produces clarity, wisdom, and peace. Rajas produces activity, desire, and restlessness. Tamas produces inertia, delusion, and sleep. The goal of yoga is to transcend all three guṇas (triguṇātīta) and rest in Puruṣa's pure consciousness.

## Governance

The concept of Prakṛti in governance: the Arthaśāstra describes the seven elements of the state (saptāṅga) as the Prakṛti of the kingdom — king, minister, territory, fort, treasury, army, ally. The concept of rāja-prakṛti (the nature of the king) — the king's guṇa-composition determines the quality of governance.

## Medicine

In Āyurveda: Prakṛti is the individual's constitutional nature — the unique combination of the three doṣas (vāta, pitta, kapha) determined at conception. The concept of deha-prakṛti (body-nature) — each person has a unique Prakṛti that determines their health tendencies. Āyurvedic treatment is tailored to the individual's Prakṛti.

## Mathematics

The concept of Prakṛti in mathematics: the three guṇas as the three fundamental operations (addition/sattva, multiplication/rajas, subtraction/tamas). The concept of Prakṛti in Bījaganita (algebra) — the term prakṛti is used for the coefficient in quadratic equations.

## Astronomy

In Jyotiṣa: the three guṇas of Prakṛti are expressed in the three types of signs (movable/rajas, fixed/tamas, dual/sattva). The concept of graha-prakṛti (planetary nature) — each planet has its own guṇa composition.

## Metallurgy

In alchemical traditions: the three guṇas of Prakṛti are expressed in the three states of matter (solid/tamas, liquid/rajas, gas/sattva). The concept of dhātu-prakṛti (metal nature) — each metal has its own guṇa composition.

## Ritual

The concept of Prakṛti in ritual: the three guṇas determine the nature of ritual offerings. Sattvic offerings (milk, ghee, fruits) are for liberation. Rajasic offerings (meat, wine) are for worldly power. Tamasic offerings are for destructive purposes. The Bhagavad Gītā (17.7-10) describes the three types of food, sacrifice, and worship according to the three guṇas.

## Symbolism

The three guṇas are symbolized by three colors: white (sattva), red (rajas), black (tamas). The three strands of a rope symbolize the three guṇas — together they bind the soul. The Goddess (Devī) symbolizes Prakṛti — the creative, sustaining, and dissolving power.

# Mantra

## Canonical Name

Mantra

## Sanskrit

मन्त्र

## Transliteration

Mantra

## Śabda

मन्त्र

## Dhātu

मन् (Man) — To think, to reflect, to contemplate.

## Vyākaraṇa

Derived from the verbal root मन् (man) with the suffix -tra (instrument suffix). Masculine noun. Pāṇini Ashtadhyayi 3.2.182 governs the -tra suffix indicating instrument of action. Mantra = that by which one thinks/contemplates (man + tra = instrument of thought).

## Nirukta

Yāska: "mantrāḥ manana-sādhanatvāt" — mantras are so called because they are instruments of contemplation. The root man (to think) combined with the instrumental suffix tra yields: that which enables or protects through thought.

## Bīja

ॐ (Om) — the mahā-bīja that is the root of all mantras. Every mantra is considered an expansion of Om. Also: specific bīja syllables (hrīṃ, klīṃ, aiṃ, etc.) are themselves mantras in condensed form.

## Tattva

Mantra-Tattva — the principle of sacred sound as a vehicle of consciousness. In Mīmāṃsā: mantras are eternal (nitya) and self-valid (svataḥ-prāmāṇya). In Kashmir Śaivism: mantra is the vibratory form of consciousness itself — Śiva's self-expression as sound. In Tantra: mantra is the sonic body of the deity.

## Śakti

Mantra-Śakti — the power inherent in sacred sound. The three aspects: Vācaka-śakti (denotative power), Vyañjaka-śakti (suggestive power), Bhāvanā-śakti (contemplative power). In Tantric tradition: the mantra is the deity's śakti in sonic form.

## Literal Meaning

Instrument of thought; that which protects through contemplation.

## Functional Meaning

Mantra is a sacred sound formula whose efficacy derives from its phonetic precision, its source in śruti (revealed scripture), and its transmission through a qualified lineage. Mantras operate at three levels: Vaikharī (audible speech), Madhyamā (mental speech), Paśyantī (visionary speech), and Parā (transcendent speech). The power of mantra is not in its semantic meaning alone but in its vibratory resonance with the structure of consciousness.

## Ontology

In Mīmāṃsā: mantras are eternal, uncreated (apauruṣeya), and self-validating. Their efficacy (apūrva) is intrinsic. In Advaita Vedānta: mantras are upāsanā (contemplative practice) tools that purify the mind for jñāna. In Kashmir Śaivism: mantra is the sonic form of Śiva's consciousness — the universe itself is mantra. In Tantra: mantra is the deity's subtle body; recitation is union with the deity.

## Cosmology

The Vedic cosmology holds that the universe was created through sound (nāda-brahman). The Ṛgveda's hymns are mantras that sustain cosmic order (ṛta). The Purāṇas describe mantras as the sonic forms of deities that govern cosmic functions. The concept of nāda-brahman (sound as Brahman) underlies the cosmological status of mantra.

## Psychology

In Yoga psychology: mantra recitation (japa) purifies the citta (mind-stuff) by replacing random mental activity with focused sound. Patañjali's Yoga Sūtras 1.27-28 describe the praṇava (Om) as the mantra of Īśvara. Mantra creates saṃskāras (impressions) that gradually transform consciousness. The concept of mantra-siddhi (mastery of mantra) describes the psychological transformation through sustained practice.

## Governance

In Vedic governance: mantras were recited at royal consecrations (rājasūya), coronations, and state rituals. The Arthaśāstra describes the use of mantras in statecraft and diplomacy. The concept of mantra-śakti (power of counsel) in governance derives from the same root — the king's council (mantra-parishad) uses the power of deliberation (manana).

## Medicine

In Āyurveda: mantra therapy (mantra-cikitsā) is a recognized treatment modality. Caraka Saṃhitā describes mantras as part of daivavyapāśraya cikitsā (divine therapy). Specific mantras are prescribed for specific conditions. The Mahāmṛtyuñjaya mantra is used for healing and longevity.

## Mathematics

The mathematical structure of mantras: Vedic meters (chandas) are mathematically precise. The Gāyatrī mantra has 24 syllables in a specific metrical pattern. The concept of mantra-gaṇita (mantra mathematics) in Tantric traditions involves precise syllable counts and arrangements.

## Astronomy

In Jyotiṣa: specific mantras are associated with each of the nine planets (navagraha). Planetary mantras are recited during specific astronomical configurations. The timing of mantra recitation (muhūrta) is determined by astronomical calculations.

## Metallurgy

In Viśvakarmā tradition: mantras are recited during the forging of sacred implements. The consecration of metal objects through mantra transforms them from material to sacred. The concept of mantra-abhiṣeka (mantra consecration) applies to ritual objects.

## Ritual

Mantra is the primary vehicle of Vedic ritual. Every ritual action is accompanied by specific mantras. The Yajurveda is primarily a collection of ritual mantras. The concept of mantra-prayoga (application of mantra) governs ritual efficacy. The sixteen saṃskāras each have specific mantras. Japa (repetition) is the primary mantra practice outside formal ritual.

## Symbolism

The spoken word as cosmic power. The bee (madhukara) symbolizes the mantra practitioner who extracts the essence of sound. The conch (śaṅkha) represents the resonance of mantra. The rosary (mālā) represents the continuous chain of mantra recitation.

# Agni

## Canonical Name

Agni

## Sanskrit

अग्नि

## Transliteration

Agni

## Śabda

अग्नि

## Dhātu

अग् (Ag) — To move tortuously; also connected to अञ्च् (Añc) — to go, to move. The root conveys the dynamic, moving nature of fire.

## Vyākaraṇa

Agni is a masculine noun, i-stem declension. One of the most frequently occurring words in the Ṛgveda (over 200 hymns addressed to Agni). Pāṇini treats Agni as a proper noun (deity name) and a common noun (fire).

## Nirukta

Yāska: "agni — agre nayati iti" — that which leads forward. Also: "agni — aṅgati iti" — that which moves. Fire is the leader, the first among the gods.

## Bīja

रं (Raṃ) — the bīja of fire (tejas) in Tantric traditions. Associated with the Maṇipūra chakra (solar plexus — the fire center).

## Tattva

Agni-Tattva — the fire principle. One of the five mahābhūtas (great elements): Pṛthvī (earth), Āp (water), Tejas/Agni (fire), Vāyu (air), Ākāśa (space). Agni is the transformative element — it converts one substance into another.

## Śakti

Tejas-Śakti — the power of radiance and transformation. Agni's śakti is the power to purify, transform, and illuminate. In Śākta traditions, Agni is the śakti of transformation (pariṇāma-śakti).

## Literal Meaning

Fire; the fire deity; the digestive fire; the cosmic transformative principle.

## Functional Meaning

Agni operates at multiple levels: (1) Physical fire — the element that transforms matter; (2) Jāṭharāgni — the digestive fire in the body; (3) Ritual fire — the medium of communication between humans and gods in yajña; (4) Cosmic fire — the transformative principle underlying all change; (5) Consciousness — Agni as the light of awareness (cit-agni).

## Ontology

In Vedic ontology: Agni is one of the three primary deities (Agni, Vāyu, Sūrya — fire, wind, sun). In Vaiśeṣika: Tejas (fire) is one of the nine dravyas (substances). In Sāṃkhya: Agni is the manifestation of the rajas guṇa — the active, transformative principle. In Tantra: Agni is the kuṇḍalinī-śakti — the fire that rises through the suṣumnā nāḍī.

## Cosmology

In Vedic cosmology: Agni is the messenger (dūta) between the human and divine realms — he carries the offerings of yajña to the gods. The three forms of Agni: Agni on earth (fire), Vāyu in the atmosphere (wind), Sūrya in the sky (sun). In Purāṇic cosmology: Agni is one of the Aṣṭadikpālas (guardians of the eight directions) — he guards the southeast.

## Psychology

Agni as psychological principle: the fire of discrimination (viveka-agni) burns away ignorance. The fire of desire (kāma-agni) is the psychological fire that must be transformed into the fire of knowledge (jñāna-agni). In Yoga psychology: the Maṇipūra chakra (fire center) governs will, power, and transformation.

## Governance

Agni in governance: the sacred fire (agni) is the witness of all royal ceremonies and oaths. The coronation ceremony (rājyābhiṣeka) involves the sacred fire. The concept of agni-parīkṣā (fire ordeal) as a test of truth in governance. The Arthaśāstra prescribes fire rituals for the protection of the kingdom.

## Medicine

In Āyurveda: Agni (digestive fire) is the central concept of health. The thirteen types of agni: jāṭharāgni (main digestive fire), five bhūtāgnis (elemental fires), seven dhātvāgnis (tissue fires). Health is balanced agni; disease is disturbed agni (sama, viṣama, tīkṣṇa, manda agni). The concept of āma (undigested toxins) arises from weak agni.

## Mathematics

In Vedic mathematics: the Agni-related altar constructions (agnicayana) required sophisticated geometry. The Śulbasūtras (altar-building manuals) contain the earliest known statements of the Pythagorean theorem, developed for constructing fire altars of precise areas.

## Astronomy

In Jyotiṣa: Agni is associated with Mars (Maṅgala) — the fiery planet. The fire signs (Meṣa/Aries, Siṃha/Leo, Dhanus/Sagittarius) are governed by Agni's principle. The concept of agni-nakṣatra (fire stars) in Vedic astronomy.

## Metallurgy

Agni is the foundation of all metallurgy — fire transforms ore into metal. The Viśvakarmā tradition treats the smith's fire as sacred — a form of Agni. The concept of agni-karma (fire-work) in metallurgy: the proper use of fire according to the dharma of each metal. Smelting, forging, and casting are all forms of agni-yoga (union through fire).

## Ritual

Agni is the central deity of Vedic ritual. The five sacred fires (pañcāgni): Gārhapatya (household fire), Āhavanīya (offering fire), Dakṣiṇāgni (southern fire), Sabhya (assembly fire), Āvasathya (guest fire). The agnihotra (daily fire offering) is the foundational Vedic ritual. The agnicayana (fire altar construction) is the most elaborate Vedic ritual, taking 12 days.

## Symbolism

Fire symbolizes transformation, purification, and illumination. The flame pointing upward symbolizes the soul's aspiration toward the divine. The three flames of the sacred fire represent the three worlds (earth, atmosphere, sky). The eternal flame (akhaṇḍa-jyoti) symbolizes the undying nature of Ātman.

## Śabda

धर्म

## Dhātu

धृ (Dhṛ) — To uphold, sustain, support.

## Vyākaraṇa

Derived from the verbal root धृ (dhṛ) with the suffix -man. Masculine noun, second declension. Pāṇini Ashtadhyayi 3.3.18 governs the suffix formation.

## Nirukta

Yāska's Nirukta: "dharayati iti dharmaḥ" — that which upholds is Dharma. The root dhṛ carries the sense of bearing, sustaining, maintaining cosmic and social order.

## Bīja

ध (Dha) — the seed syllable associated with sustaining force in Tantric traditions.

## Tattva

Ṛta-Dharma Tattva — the principle of cosmic and moral order that sustains all existence. In Sāṃkhya: Dharma is a quality (guṇa) of the Mahat (cosmic intellect). In Vedānta: Dharma is the expression of Ṛta at the human level.

## Śakti

Dharma-Śakti — the preserving and ordering power. Associated with Viṣṇu's sustaining function (sthiti-śakti). In Śākta traditions, Dharma is upheld by the Goddess as Mahāmāyā maintaining cosmic law.

## Literal Meaning

That which is upheld; that which upholds. The sustaining principle.

## Functional Meaning

Dharma is the universal principle governing righteous conduct, cosmic order, social duty, and individual ethics. It operates simultaneously at four levels: Ṛta (cosmic order), Varṇāśrama-dharma (social order), Svadharma (individual duty), and Sādhāraṇa-dharma (universal ethics applicable to all beings).

## Ontology

In Vaiśeṣika: Dharma is a padārtha (category of reality) — the cause of abhyudaya (worldly prosperity) and niḥśreyasa (liberation). In Mīmāṃsā: Dharma is codanā-lakṣaṇa — that which is enjoined by Vedic injunction. In Advaita Vedānta: Dharma at the vyāvahārika (conventional) level is real and necessary; at the pāramārthika (absolute) level, only Brahman exists.

## Cosmology

Dharma is one of the four Puruṣārthas (aims of human life): Dharma, Artha, Kāma, Mokṣa. In the Purāṇic cosmology, Dharma is personified as a deity, son of Brahmā, husband of ten daughters of Dakṣa. In the four yugas (Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, Kali), Dharma stands on four legs, three, two, and one respectively — indicating progressive decline of cosmic order.

## Psychology

In Yoga psychology (Patañjali): Dharma-megha-samādhi is the highest samādhi, the "cloud of virtue" that rains liberation. Dharma as psychological principle governs the sattva-rajas-tamas balance in the individual. Right action (dharmic action) produces psychological clarity (citta-prasāda).

## Governance

Rājadharma (royal duty) is elaborated in Manusmṛti, Arthaśāstra, Mahābhārata Śāntiparva. The king's primary duty is dharma-rakṣaṇa (protection of dharma). Kauṭilya's Arthaśāstra treats dharma as the foundation of statecraft. Aśoka's dhamma edicts represent the historical application of dharmic governance.

## Medicine

In Āyurveda: Dharma is the foundation of Āyurvedic ethics. The physician's svadharma includes ahiṃsā (non-harm), satya (truth), and service. Caraka Saṃhitā Sūtrasthāna 1.15 states that the physician who follows dharma achieves both worldly success and liberation.

## Mathematics

Dharma as cosmic order underlies the mathematical precision of Vedic ritual geometry (Śulbasūtras). The Pythagorean theorem appears in Baudhāyana Śulbasūtra as a dharmic requirement for altar construction. Mathematical truth (satya) is considered a form of dharma.

## Astronomy

Ṛta (cosmic order, precursor to dharma) governs the movements of celestial bodies. Vedic astronomy (Jyotiṣa) treats planetary motion as dharmic — planets follow their ordained paths. The concept of ṛtu (season) derives from ṛta, linking dharma to astronomical cycles.

## Metallurgy

In Viśvakarmā tradition: the dharma of metals is their inherent nature and proper use. Gold (suvarṇa) has the dharma of purity; iron (ayasa) has the dharma of strength. Proper metallurgical practice follows the dharma of each material.

## Ritual

Yajña (sacrifice) is the primary ritual expression of dharma. The Mīmāṃsā school holds that Vedic ritual injunctions (vidhi) define dharma. Dharma-śāstra prescribes the sixteen saṃskāras (life-cycle rituals) as the ritual framework of dharmic life. Sandhyāvandana (daily worship) is the minimal dharmic ritual obligation.

## Symbolism

Dharma is symbolized by the wheel (dharmacakra) — the Buddha's first teaching is the "turning of the wheel of dharma." The scales of justice represent dharma's balancing function. The lotus represents dharma's purity amid worldly existence. The cow (go) is the living symbol of dharma in Vedic tradition.

## Traditional Interpretations

- Advaita Vedānta (Śaṅkara): Dharma is ultimately subsumed in jñāna (knowledge); it is a means, not the end
- Viśiṣṭādvaita (Rāmānuja): Dharma is bhakti-yoga — devotional service to Viṣṇu is the highest dharma
- Dvaita (Madhva): Dharma is the eternal will of Viṣṇu; individual dharma is participation in divine order
- Mīmāṃsā (Jaimini): Dharma is exclusively Vedic injunction; no dharma exists outside Veda
- Buddhism: Dharma is the teaching of the Buddha and the nature of reality (dhamma)
- Jainism: Dharma is the medium of motion (one of the six dravyas); also righteous conduct (dharma)

## Historical Evolution

- Ṛgvedic period: Ṛta (cosmic order) is the precursor; dharma appears rarely
- Atharvaveda: Dharma begins to acquire social and ethical dimensions
- Upaniṣadic period: Dharma becomes internalized as ethical-spiritual principle
- Epic period (Mahābhārata): Dharma becomes the central problematic — the Gītā's entire teaching is dharmic
- Dharmaśāstra period (200 BCE–1200 CE): Systematic codification of dharma in law texts
- Colonial period: Dharma reinterpreted through encounter with Western legal concepts
- Modern: Dharma as "religion" (mistranslation) vs. dharma as cosmic-ethical principle (ongoing debate)

# Yajna

## Canonical Name

Yajna

## Sanskrit

यज्ञ

## Transliteration

Yajña

## Śabda

यज्ञ

## Dhātu

यज् (Yaj) — To worship, to sacrifice, to offer.

## Vyākaraṇa

Yajña is a masculine noun derived from the root yaj (to worship/sacrifice) with the suffix -na. The root yaj is one of the most important roots in Vedic Sanskrit — it gives yajña (sacrifice), yajus (sacrificial formula), yajamāna (sacrificer), and Yajurveda (the Veda of sacrificial formulas).

## Nirukta

Yāska: "yajyate devā anena iti yajñaḥ" — that by which the gods are worshipped. Yajña is the act of offering that creates and maintains the relationship between humans and the divine.

## Bīja

ॐ (Om) — the primordial offering. Also स्वाहा (Svāhā) — the mantra of offering in fire rituals.

## Tattva

Yajña-Tattva — the principle of sacred exchange and cosmic reciprocity. The universe itself is a yajña — a continuous cycle of giving and receiving between all levels of existence.

## Śakti

Yajña-Śakti — the power of sacred offering. The śakti that maintains the cosmic order through the cycle of giving.

## Literal Meaning

Sacrifice; offering; worship; the sacred act of giving.

## Functional Meaning

Yajña is the foundational principle of Vedic civilization — the sacred act of offering that maintains cosmic order (ṛta). The Bhagavad Gītā (3.10-16) describes yajña as the cosmic cycle: Brahmā created beings along with yajña; through yajña, rain falls; from rain, food grows; from food, beings live; beings perform yajña — the wheel of cosmic reciprocity. Yajña operates at five levels: Brahma-yajña (study of Vedas), Deva-yajña (fire offerings to gods), Pitṛ-yajña (offerings to ancestors), Bhūta-yajña (offerings to all beings), Manuṣya-yajña (hospitality to humans).

## Ontology

In Mīmāṃsā: yajña is the primary means of achieving all human goals — dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. The apūrva (unseen potency) of yajña persists until it bears fruit. In Advaita: yajña at the highest level is the offering of the ego into the fire of knowledge (jñāna-yajña). In the Bhagavad Gītā: karma-yoga is yajña — all action performed without attachment is an offering to the divine.

## Cosmology

In Vedic cosmology: the universe itself was created through a cosmic yajña — the Puruṣa Sūkta (Ṛgveda 10.90) describes the primordial sacrifice of the cosmic Puruṣa from which all creation emerged. The concept of yajña as the mechanism of cosmic maintenance — the gods depend on yajña for their sustenance.

## Psychology

Yajña as psychological principle: the offering of the ego (ahaṃkāra) into the fire of self-knowledge is the highest yajña. The Bhagavad Gītā (4.24-33) describes multiple forms of yajña as psychological practices: offering the senses into the fire of restraint, offering actions into the fire of knowledge.

## Governance

Rāja-sūya (royal consecration) and Aśvamedha (horse sacrifice) are the primary royal yajñas. The king's yajña maintains the prosperity of the kingdom. The concept of rāṣṭra-yajña (national sacrifice) — governance as a form of yajña for the welfare of all.

## Medicine

In Āyurveda: yajña smoke (dhūpa) is used for purification and healing. The concept of yajña as environmental medicine — fire offerings purify the atmosphere. Modern research on yajña smoke (homa therapy) suggests antimicrobial properties.

## Mathematics

The Śulbasūtras (altar-building manuals) contain the earliest known mathematical theorems, developed for constructing yajña altars of precise areas. The Pythagorean theorem, geometric transformations, and irrational numbers appear in the context of yajña altar construction.

## Astronomy

The timing of yajñas is determined by Jyotiṣa (Vedic astronomy). The concept of muhūrta (auspicious time) for yajña is based on astronomical calculations. The Nakṣatra system was developed partly for determining the correct times for yajña.

## Metallurgy

The sacred fire (agni) of yajña is the basis of all metallurgical fire. The concept of dhātu-yajña (offering of metals) — specific metals are offered in specific yajñas for specific results.

## Ritual

The five mahāyajñas (great sacrifices): Brahma-yajña, Deva-yajña, Pitṛ-yajña, Bhūta-yajña, Manuṣya-yajña. The Soma yajña (Agniṣṭoma, Vājapeya, Rājasūya) are the major Vedic sacrifices. The agnihotra (daily fire offering) is the minimal yajña obligation.

## Symbolism

The fire symbolizes yajña — the transformative medium of offering. The smoke rising from the fire symbolizes the offering reaching the divine realm. The svāhā (offering mantra) symbolizes the act of giving without reservation.

## Related Deities

- Agni (the fire deity — the medium of yajña)
- Indra (the primary recipient of Soma offerings)
- Viṣṇu (Yajña is one of Viṣṇu's names — he is the cosmic sacrifice)
- Brahmā (the creator who established yajña)

## Related Lokas

- Svarga (heaven — the destination of yajña's merit)
- Pitṛloka (the realm of ancestors — maintained by Pitṛ-yajña)

## Related Koshas

- Prāṇamaya Kosha (energy sheath) — the field of prāṇa-yajña (offering of breath)
- Annamaya Kosha (physical sheath) — the field of physical offerings

- Anāhata (heart chakra) — the seat of bhakti-yajña (devotional offering)
